title: Krishna's Dawn Worship in Dwaraka
one_line_summary: Krishna rises in the brahma-muhurta, performs his ablutions, worships the Lord within, gives daily gifts of cows and wealth to brahmanas, and blesses his people.
source_excerpt: Waking with Rukmini at his side, Krishna bathes, meditates on the self-effulgent Brahman, performs the sandhya rites, and each day gives herds of milk-giving cows with golden horns to brahmanas. He then adorns himself, mounts his chariot, and enters the Sudharma assembly hall surrounded by the Yadus. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1-19)

title: The Captive Kings Appeal to Krishna
one_line_summary: A royal messenger arrives in Krishna's assembly and reports that Jarasandha has imprisoned twenty thousand defeated kings in Girivraja, who beg Krishna for release.
source_excerpt: A man of extraordinary appearance is admitted before Krishna and, with joined palms, tells how Jarasandha has forcibly imprisoned the kings who refused to submit to his conquest, twenty thousand of them in Girivraja. The captive kings declare they have taken refuge in Krishna from the terror of worldly existence. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 20-30)

title: Narada Announces the Rajasuya
one_line_summary: Narada arrives at the assembly and announces that Yudhishthira will perform the Rajasuya sacrifice, requesting Krishna's consent and presence.
source_excerpt: The divine sage Narada, radiant with matted tawny locks, appears in the assembly and is honored by Krishna. He announces that Krishna's cousin Yudhishthira, desiring imperial sovereignty, will worship Krishna with the Rajasuya sacrifice, and that Krishna should consent. Krishna then playfully asks Uddhava for his counsel. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 31-46)

title: Uddhava's Counsel to Slay Jarasandha
one_line_summary: Uddhava advises Krishna that the Rajasuya requires conquering the directions, and that Jarasandha — who can only be killed by Bhima in single combat — must first be destroyed.
source_excerpt: Uddhava counsels that the Rajasuya is to be performed by one who has conquered all directions, so defeating Jarasandha serves both purposes. Since Jarasandha is the equal of Bhima alone and cannot be overthrown with an army, Bhima should go to him disguised as a brahmana, request single combat, and slay him before Krishna. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1-10)
variant_notes: VARIANT of the Rajasuya slaying-plan: Bhagavata Purana attributes the plan to Uddhava's counsel; Mahabharata 2.20 presents Krishna himself proposing it. Attribution difference is material — kept as separate stories.

title: Krishna's Grand Procession from Dwaraka
one_line_summary: Krishna departs Dwaraka for Indraprastha with a vast army, chariots, elephants and his queens, to the sound of drums and conches.
source_excerpt: Krishna orders the departure, entrusts Dwaraka to Balarama, and mounts his Garuda-bannered chariot. Surrounded by an immense army with resounding drums, conches and trumpets, and followed by his queens in their conveyances, he sets out, crossing many lands, rivers and towns on the way to Indraprastha. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 11-21)

title: Reunion with the Pandavas and Kunti
one_line_summary: Krishna arrives at Indraprastha, where Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, the twins and Kunti embrace him with overflowing love.
source_excerpt: Hearing of Krishna's arrival, Yudhishthira comes out with his preceptors and friends, and embraces Krishna again and again with tears of joy. Bhima, Arjuna and the twins also embrace him; Kunti rises from her couch and embraces her nephew, and Draupadi honors the queens Rukmini, Satyabhama, Bhadra and Jambavati. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 22-44)

title: Yudhishthira Requests the Rajasuya
one_line_summary: Yudhishthira asks Krishna's permission and blessing to perform the Rajasuya, and Krishna approves, promising to win the kings of the earth for him.
source_excerpt: Yudhishthira declares his wish to perform the purifying Rajasuya sacrifice and asks Krishna, the lord of all, to bring it about. Krishna approves, saying that after conquering all the kings and gathering the requisites the sacrifice should be performed, and that none can surpass Yudhishthira in splendor, not even the gods. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1-10)

title: The Pandavas Conquer the Directions
one_line_summary: Yudhishthira sends his four brothers to conquer the four quarters, and they return laden with tribute for the sacrifice.
source_excerpt: Pleased, Yudhishthira dispatches his brothers on the conquest of the quarters — Sahadeva to the south, Nakula to the west, Arjuna to the north, and Bhima to the east. They vanquish the kings and bring back abundant wealth for the sacrifice. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 11-13)

title: Approaching Jarasandha in Disguise
one_line_summary: Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna travel to Girivraja disguised as brahmanas and ask Jarasandha for alms, testing his charity.
source_excerpt: Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna, wearing the marks of brahmanas, go to Girivraja where Jarasandha dwells. They arrive at the hour of hospitality and ask the generous king, famed for giving even his own head to suppliants, to grant them what they desire. Jarasandha, recognizing them by their voices and marks, resolves to give whatever they ask. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 14-26)

title: Jarasandha Taunts Krishna
one_line_summary: Krishna reveals their true identities and asks for single combat; Jarasandha laughs, taunts Krishna as a coward who fled Mathura, and chooses Bhima as his opponent.
source_excerpt: Krishna tells Jarasandha they have come seeking battle, and reveals that the man is Bhima, the other Arjuna, and himself Krishna, his enemy. Jarasandha laughs aloud and taunts that he will not fight Krishna, a coward who abandoned Mathura and fled to the sea, but that Bhima is his match in strength. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 27-32)

title: The Mace-Duel of Bhima and Jarasandha
one_line_summary: Bhima and Jarasandha fight an indecisive mace-duel, exchanging blows that crush their clubs, then striking with iron-hard fists.
source_excerpt: Taking up their great maces, the two heroes clash outside the city, circling in intricate patterns like wrestlers. Their clubs shatter under the force of their blows, and enraged they strike each other with fists hard as iron, the sound like thunder, yet the fight of the equal champions remains indecisive. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 33-38)

title: Krishna's Signal: Jarasandha Split in Two
one_line_summary: Knowing Jarasandha's birth secret, Krishna signals by splitting a twig; Bhima tears Jarasandha in two and kills him.
source_excerpt: Knowing his enemy's birth and death, Krishna, wishing to show Bhima the means, splits a twig in two as a sign. Bhima understands, seizes Jarasandha by the feet, throws him down, and tearing him apart kills him, upon which a great cry of lamentation arises. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 39-44)

title: Sahadeva Crowned and the Kings Freed
one_line_summary: Krishna crowns Jarasandha's son Sahadeva king of Magadha and releases all the kings imprisoned by Jarasandha.
source_excerpt: Krishna installs Jarasandha's son Sahadeva as lord of the Magadhas, and releases the kings who had been held captive by Jarasandha. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 45)

title: The Liberated Kings Behold Krishna
one_line_summary: Twenty thousand eight hundred freed kings emerge from the mountain prison, behold Krishna's form, praise him, receive his teaching, and are sent home with honor.
source_excerpt: The released kings, emaciated and haggard, gaze upon Krishna's dark four-armed form and bow at his feet in gratitude. Krishna assures them their devotion to him will be firm, bids them rule their realms righteously, has them bathed, feasted and adorned, and sends them home with chariots and kind words. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1-29)

title: Krishna Receives the First Honor
one_line_summary: Sahadeva declares Krishna alone worthy of the highest honor at the sacrifice, and Yudhishthira washes Krishna's feet and worships him before all.
source_excerpt: Sahadeva declares that Krishna alone, the lord of the Satvatas in whom all deities and all sacrifice abide, deserves the foremost honor. At this the whole assembly approves, and Yudhishthira, overwhelmed with love, washes Krishna's feet, bears the water on his head, and worships him with garments and jewels. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 17-28)

title: Shishupala's Outburst
one_line_summary: Enraged at Krishna's honor, Shishupala rises and heaps insults on Krishna, calling him a cowherd unworthy of worship; the assembly rebukes him and some draw weapons.
source_excerpt: Shishupala, son of Damaghosha, rises from his seat in fury and abuses Krishna, saying a cowherd who abandoned his caste cannot be honored while the great sages are present. The assembled sages stop their ears and curse him, and the enraged Pandavas and their allies rise with weapons to slay him. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 29-41)

title: Krishna Slays Shishupala
one_line_summary: Krishna, restraining his own men, cuts off Shishupala's head with the sharp-edged discus, and Shishupala's effulgence merges into Krishna.
source_excerpt: Restraining his followers, Krishna rises and with his razor-edged discus severs the head of the rushing Shishupala. A great uproar follows, and before the eyes of all beings a brilliant light issuing from Shishupala's body enters Krishna, as he who had meditated on Krishna in enmity through three births attained oneness with him. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 42-45)

title: The Rajasuya Completed
one_line_summary: Krishna completes the Rajasuya for Yudhishthira, gives the priests their fees, stays some months, and departs; only Duryodhana cannot bear the Pandavas' splendor.
source_excerpt: Krishna, lord of the lords of yoga, completes the sacrifice, bestows ample fees on the priests, and after some months takes leave of the reluctant Yudhishthira and returns to his own city. All the assembled guests depart praising Krishna and the sacrifice, except the wicked Duryodhana, who could not endure the Pandavas' prosperity. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 46-52)

title: Duryodhana's Humiliation in Maya's Hall
one_line_summary: In the illusory assembly hall built by Maya, Duryodhana mistakes water for floor and falls; Bhima and the women laugh, and Duryodhana departs burning with shame and hatred.
source_excerpt: In the wondrous hall built by Maya, Duryodhana mistakes a crystal floor for water and lifts his garment, then falls where he thought the floor was, deceived by the illusion. Bhima and the women laugh despite the king's restraint, and Duryodhana, humiliated and blazing with rage, departs in silence, while Krishna remains silent, intent on relieving the earth's burden. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 30-38)

title: Shalva Wins the Flying City Saubha
one_line_summary: Shalva, friend of the slain Shishupala, vows to destroy the Yadavas and wins from Shiva through austere penance the flying iron city Saubha, built by Maya.
source_excerpt: Shalva, friend of Shishupala, who had been defeated at Rukmini's wedding, vows before the kings to make the earth devoid of Yadavas. To this end he worships the lord Shiva, eating a handful of dust each day, and after a year Shiva, easily pleased, offers him a boon. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1-7)

title: Shalva Besieges Dwaraka
one_line_summary: Shalva arrives at Dwaraka in the indestructible flying city Saubha and rains weapons, rocks and serpents upon the city, terrifying its people.
source_excerpt: Obtaining the self-moving, impenetrable vehicle Saubha, Shalva flies to Dwaraka remembering the enmity of the Vrishnis, and with a vast army shatters its gardens and gates, raining weapons, rocks, trees and serpents upon the city. Pradyumna, seeing his people afflicted, mounts his chariot and cries 'Do not fear,' and the Yadava warriors sally forth. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 7-16)

title: Pradyumna's Valor and Wounding
one_line_summary: Pradyumna destroys Shalva's illusions and slays many foes, but is struck senseless by Dyuman's mace; recovering, he rebukes his charioteer for drawing him from the field.
source_excerpt: Pradyumna in a moment dispels the demon's illusions with divine weapons and showers arrows on Shalva's host, winning the admiration of both armies. But Dyuman, Shalva's minister, strikes Pradyumna on the chest with his mace, and the charioteer carries the senseless hero away; regaining consciousness, Pradyumna rebukes him, saying no Yadu may be seen fleeing the field. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 17-32)

title: Krishna Returns to the Battle
one_line_summary: Returning from Indraprastha and seeing evil omens, Krishna hurries to Dwaraka, orders his chariot against Shalva, and joins the fight, shattering Shalva's weapons.
source_excerpt: Krishna, summoned to Indraprastha for the Rajasuya, returns to Dwaraka perceiving dire omens, and realizing the Chaidya's allies have attacked his city, orders Daruka to drive his chariot against Shalva. Shalva hurls a blazing spear at Krishna's charioteer, which Krishna cuts to a hundred pieces with his arrows, and he pierces Shalva with sixteen shafts. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 5-18)

title: The Illusion of Vasudeva's Death
one_line_summary: Shalva conjures the illusion that his men have captured and beheaded Vasudeva before Krishna's eyes; Krishna, briefly appearing grief-stricken, then sees through the sorcery.
source_excerpt: A man appears weeping and tells Krishna that Shalva has carried off his father Vasudeva like an animal, and Shalva then seems to behead Vasudeva before Krishna, taunting him to save him if he can. Krishna, adopting a human mood, appears bewildered for a moment, then perceives it to be the demon's sorcery wrought by Maya, and seeing neither messenger nor his father's body, prepares to destroy the enemy. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 19-31)
variant_notes: The text itself notes (verse 29) that some sages do not accept this account of Krishna's momentary grief, since sorrow and delusion cannot touch the Lord.

title: Krishna Destroys Saubha and Slays Shalva
one_line_summary: Krishna cuts off Shalva's arm, shatters the flying city Saubha with his mace, and beheads Shalva with the discus as he attacks on foot.
source_excerpt: Krishna pierces the rushing Shalva with arrows, cuts through his armor, bow and crest-jewel, and crushes the city Saubha to pieces with his mace, so that it falls into the water in a thousand fragments. Then, as Shalva charges on foot with his mace, Krishna severs his arm and, wielding his wondrous discus blazing like the sun at world's end, cuts off his crowned head. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 32-35)

title: Krishna Slays Dantavakra and Viduratha
one_line_summary: Dantavakra attacks Krishna with a mace to avenge Shishupala and Shalva; Krishna crushes his chest, then beheads his brother Viduratha with the discus.
source_excerpt: Dantavakra, eager to repay his slain friends, rushes at Krishna on foot, taunting him as the murderer of his kinsmen, and strikes him on the head with his mace. Unshaken, Krishna crushes Dantavakra's chest with his mace Kaumodaki, and when his brother Viduratha comes on to avenge him, Krishna severs his crowned head with the discus. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1-11)

title: Balarama Slays the Suta Romaharshana
one_line_summary: At Naimisha, Balarama, seeing the suta Romaharshana seated without rising to honor the sages, kills him with a blade of kusha grass; the sages cry out that he has committed brahma-hatya.
source_excerpt: Visiting the sages' sacrifice at Naimisha, Balarama sees the suta Romaharshana, a shudra by birth, seated among the brahmanas without rising to honor them. Enraged, Balarama strikes him down with a blade of kusha grass, and the sages cry out that he has committed the sin of slaying a brahmana, saying this was done without knowledge and must be expiated. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 15-31)
notes: Note: this is Balarama's own transgression (brahma-hatya), not the sages' curse that later dooms the Yadavas — that occurs in Canto 11.

title: The Sages Prescribe Balarama's Penance
one_line_summary: The sages instruct Balarama that to expiate the brahmana-slaying he must slay the demon Balvala, who defiles their sacrifice, and then perform a year-long pilgrimage.
source_excerpt: The sages tell Balarama that his atonement is to slay the cruel demon Balvala, son of Ilvala, who rains filth upon their sacrifice at every parvan, and then to wander Bharatavarsha bathing at the sacred fords for twelve months to be purified. Balarama accepts, undertaking the expiation for the world's benefit. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 32-39)

title: Balarama Slays the Demon Balvala
one_line_summary: When Balvala appears at the sacrifice raining impurity, Balarama drags him down with his plough and crushes his head with his mace, and the sages shower Balarama with honors.
source_excerpt: At the next parvan the terrible demon Balvala appears, raining filth upon the sacrificial hall. Balarama, remembering his plough and mace, drags the sky-roaming Balvala down with the plough's tip and crushes his skull with the mace, and the delighted sages honor Balarama and bestow blessings, a celestial garland and garments upon him. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1-8)

title: Balarama Tries to Halt the Mace-Duel
one_line_summary: Hearing that Bhima and Duryodhana are locked in their final mace-duel, Balarama goes to stop the slaughter but, unable to part the two, returns to Dwaraka.
source_excerpt: Hearing of the battle of the Kurus and Pandavas and the slaughter of the warrior kings, Balarama, deeming the earth's burden lifted, goes to the field where Bhima and Duryodhana are fighting with maces. He tells the equal champions that neither can win and to desist, but the two, bound by enmity and remembering mutual insults, do not heed his words, and Balarama, accepting it as destiny, returns to Dwaraka. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 21-28)

title: Sudama's Poverty and Journey
one_line_summary: Sudama's wife urges the destitute brahmana to seek his boyhood friend Krishna, and he sets out for Dwaraka with a humble gift of flat rice.
source_excerpt: Sudama, a learned and self-controlled brahmana living in great poverty, is urged by his devoted wife to visit Krishna, his boyhood friend who now dwells in Dwaraka, saying Krishna will give them wealth. She borrows four handfuls of flattened rice and ties them in a rag as a gift, and Sudama sets out for Dwaraka wondering how he may gain sight of Krishna. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 5-16)

title: Krishna Embraces His Old Friend
one_line_summary: Krishna rises from his couch, embraces Sudama with tears of joy, washes his feet, and anoints him, while Rukmini fans him, astonishing the palace women.
source_excerpt: Seeing Sudama from afar, Krishna rises from Rukmini's couch, runs to him, and embraces his old friend with tears of joy, then seats him on his own couch, washes his feet and bears the water on his head. The goddess Rukmini herself fans the emaciated brahmana, and the women of the palace marvel at the honor shown to a poor mendicant. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 16-26)

title: Memories of the Gurukula
one_line_summary: Krishna and Sudama recall their student days under Sandipani, when they were sent to fetch firewood and, caught in a fierce storm, wandered lost until the guru found them at dawn.
source_excerpt: Krishna asks Sudama whether he remembers their days serving the guru, and recounts how, sent by the guru's wife to gather firewood, they entered the forest when a violent wind and rain arose, night fell, and, lost in the darkness and holding hands, they wandered till the guru found them at sunrise and blessed them. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 27-42)

title: Krishna Eats Sudama's Flat Rice
one_line_summary: Krishna asks for the gift and eats Sudama's handful of flat rice with delight, and Sudama, too ashamed to ask for anything, returns home empty-handed.
source_excerpt: Krishna asks his friend what gift he has brought, saying even a trifle offered with love pleases him, and taking the flattened rice from Sudama's robe, eats one handful and reaches for a second — but the goddess of fortune, pleased, stays his hand, saying this much suffices to grant all riches. Sudama spends the night, and returns home without asking Krishna for any wealth. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 2-12)

title: Sudama Finds His Hut a Palace
one_line_summary: Returning home, Sudama finds his poor dwelling transformed into a celestial palace and his wife radiant, and he reflects that this is Krishna's unasked grace.
source_excerpt: Reaching his home, Sudama finds it surrounded by celestial mansions with gardens and lakes, his wife radiant like the goddess of fortune among her attendants, and his house become a palace with golden couches and jeweled lamps. He reflects that the Lord, knowing wealth would make him forget, gave him prosperity unasked, and that Krishna treasured even his single handful of rice. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 13-37)

title: The Pilgrimage to Samanta-panchaka
one_line_summary: On the occasion of a solar eclipse, the Yadavas journey to Samanta-panchaka to bathe and give gifts, and there a vast reunion of kings and kinsfolk takes place.
source_excerpt: A great solar eclipse occurs, and the Yadavas, together with Vasudeva, Akrura and others, journey to Samanta-panchaka, the field where Rama had once made lakes of the kings' blood, to bathe and give cows and gifts. There they meet the kings of many realms and their own long-separated kin, and embrace one another with tears of joy. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1-15)

title: Reunion with Nanda and Yashoda
one_line_summary: Nanda and the cowherds arrive, and Krishna, Balarama, Yashoda, Devaki and Rohini embrace one another, recalling the old days in Gokula.
source_excerpt: Nanda arrives with the cowherds to see Krishna, and the Vrishnis embrace him as if life itself had returned. Krishna and Balarama bow to their parents and, speechless with love, embrace them; Yashoda takes her two sons on her lap, and Devaki and Rohini, remembering the friendship of old, embrace Yashoda and speak of the love shown to the boys in Gokula. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 30-37)

title: Krishna's Counsel to the Gopis
one_line_summary: Krishna meets the gopis, who have long pined for him, embraces them, and teaches them that all beings abide in him, and that their love for him grants immortality.
source_excerpt: The gopis, seeing Krishna after so long, embrace him in their hearts and attain that state which even the ever-yoked cannot easily gain. Krishna asks whether they remember his friendship, and teaches them that as the wind scatters clouds, so the Lord unites and separates beings, and that devotion to him grants immortality — by which instruction the gopis, their bondage dissolved, attained him. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 38-47)

title: Krishna Wins Lakshmana at Her Svayamvara
one_line_summary: In the queens' accounts of their marriages, Lakshmana tells how Krishna strung a great bow, shot down the fish target, and bore her away, defeating the rival kings.
source_excerpt: Asked by Draupadi how Krishna married them, Lakshmana recounts that her father arranged a svayamvara with a fish target, at which kings from everywhere failed even to string the bow. Krishna took up the bow, strung it effortlessly, and with a single arrow shot the fish, and when the envious kings attacked he cut them down with his arrows and carried Lakshmana to Dwaraka. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 16-38)
notes: Retrospective narration by the queens; the other queens' marriage accounts (Rukmini, Satyabhama, Jambavati, Kalindi, Mitravinda, Satya, Bhadra) repeat episodes covered in earlier chapters and are not separately indexed.

title: Vasudeva's Sacrifice
one_line_summary: The sages, pleased with Vasudeva's question, initiate him and he performs a great sacrifice at Samanta-panchaka, with his sons and the Yadavas attending.
source_excerpt: Vasudeva, instructed by the sages, chooses them as his priests, and they initiate him and perform sacrifices at that holy field. Krishna and Balarama shine there among their kinsmen and sons, and after the rites Vasudeva gives rich gifts of cows, land and maidens to the priests, completing the sacrifice with the avabhritha bath. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 42-55)

title: Nanda's Farewell
one_line_summary: Vasudeva, overcome with love, laments that riches blinded him to old friends, and Nanda, honored by the Yadavas with rich gifts, departs for Mathura with the cowherds.
source_excerpt: Vasudeva, weeping as he recalls the friendship, tells Nanda that the snare called affection is hard to cast off, and that blinded by royal splendor he neglected his old friend. Nanda stays three months, honored by the Yadavas, and then, laden with rich gifts from Vasudeva, Ugrasena, Krishna and Uddhava, departs with the cowherds, his heart fixed on Krishna's lotus feet. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 58-69)

title: Devaki Asks for Her Slain Sons
one_line_summary: Devaki, remembering the six sons Kamsa killed, tearfully asks Krishna and Balarama to bring back her dead children.
source_excerpt: Hearing of how Krishna and Balarama had brought back their guru's son, Devaki, remembering the sons slaughtered by Kamsa, tearfully asks them to grant her wish to see her slain children restored. She recalls that they had once fetched their guru's dead son as a fee, and entreats them to bring back the sons slain by the Bhoja king. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 26-32)

title: Krishna and Balarama Visit Bali in Sutala
one_line_summary: Krishna and Balarama descend to Sutala, where Bali, the daitya king, receives them with great devotion, and Krishna reveals the true origin of Devaki's six sons.
source_excerpt: Entering Sutala by their yoga-maya, Krishna and Balarama are received by the daitya king Bali, who rises, bows, and washes their feet with his kin. Krishna then reveals that the six sons were once the six sons of Marichi, who laughed at Brahma and were cursed to be born as demons — the very children Kamsa killed, who now dwell nearby awaiting release. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 33-51)

title: The Six Sons Restored to Devaki
one_line_summary: Krishna and Balarama bring the six sons back from Sutala; Devaki nurses them with her milk, and, released from the curse, they bow and ascend to the gods' abode.
source_excerpt: Taking the six sons, Krishna and Balarama return to Dwaraka and give them to their mother, and Devaki, her breasts flowing with milk, nurses and embraces them. Having drunk her milk, they bow to Krishna, Devaki, Vasudeva and Balarama, and before the eyes of all beings ascend to the abode of the gods. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 51-56)

title: Arjuna Abducts Subhadra
one_line_summary: Arjuna, disguised as a renunciant, wins Krishna's sister Subhadra and carries her off; when Balarama grows angry, Krishna pacifies him and he sends wedding gifts.
source_excerpt: Arjuna, on pilgrimage, hears that Balarama intends to give their sister Subhadra to Duryodhana, and going to Dwaraka disguised as a tridandi renunciant, wins Subhadra's heart and carries her off on his chariot during a festival. Balarama grows furious, but Krishna pacifies him, and Balarama, appeased, sends rich wedding gifts for the bride and groom. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1-11)

title: Krishna Visits Shrutadeva and Bahulashva
one_line_summary: Krishna, to please both the sage Shrutadeva and King Bahulashva of Mithila, visits both their homes simultaneously, unseen by each other.
source_excerpt: Krishna travels to Mithila with the sages, and both the brahmana Shrutadeva and King Bahulashva, each thinking Krishna has come to his own house, invite him and the sages. To please both devotees, Krishna enters both homes at once, unseen by either, and each worships him with overflowing devotion. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 23-36)

title: Vrikasura's Lethal Boon from Shiva
one_line_summary: The asura Vrikasura wins from Shiva the boon that whoever's head he touches will die, then tries to test it on Shiva himself, who flees in terror to Vaikuntha.
source_excerpt: The asura Vrikasura, son of Shakuni, performs terrible penance and wins from the compassionate Shiva the boon that whomever he touches on the head shall die. To test it, he tries to place his hand on Shiva's own head, and the terrified Shiva, pursued by the asura, flees to the ends of the earth and heavens and finally takes refuge in Vaikuntha. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 12-27)
notes: Vishnu-centric narrative told within Canto 10 (Krishna as the Supreme Lord Vishnu).

title: Vishnu Saves Shiva from Vrikasura
one_line_summary: Vishnu, appearing as a young brahmachari, tricks Vrikasura into touching his own head, and the asura destroys himself, freeing Shiva.
source_excerpt: Vishnu, taking the form of a radiant young brahmachari, receives the exhausted Vrikasura and, feigning disbelief in Shiva's boon, tells him to test it by placing his hand on his own head. The bewildered asura does so and instantly splits his own skull and dies, while the gods shower flowers and the freed Shiva praises Vishnu, the deliverer of those who offend the great. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 28-38)

title: Bhrigu Tests the Three Gods
one_line_summary: Sent by the sages to test who is greatest, Bhrigu finds Brahma and Shiva angered, but Vishnu, far from being offended, apologizes and serves him, proving Vishnu supreme.
source_excerpt: To settle which of the three gods is greatest, the sages send Bhrigu; Brahma grows angry at Bhrigu's disrespect but restrains himself, and Shiva raises his trident to slay him till the goddess intervenes. Vishnu, however, on being kicked in the chest by Bhrigu, rises and apologizes, asking the sage to forgive him — and Bhrigu, moved, declares Vishnu alone the abode of peace and fearlessness. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1-18)

title: The Brahmana's Dying Sons
one_line_summary: In Dwaraka, a brahmana's newborn sons die one after another; he lays their bodies at the palace gate and laments the king's failure to protect his subjects.
source_excerpt: A brahmana's infant sons die as soon as they touch the ground, and each time he lays the dead child at the palace gate, lamenting that the king's fault has slain his children. He accuses the unrighteous ruler of failing in his duty, so that his subjects perish in misery. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 20-27)

title: Arjuna's Failed Vow
one_line_summary: Arjuna boasts that he will protect the brahmana's next child, but though he fences the delivery-room with arrows, the newborn vanishes, and the brahmana rebukes him.
source_excerpt: Arjuna, hearing the brahmana's lament, vows that he will protect the next child or enter fire, and when the time comes he rings the delivery-room with a cage of arrows. But the newborn vanishes bodily into the sky, and the brahmana mocks Arjuna, saying that even Balarama, Krishna, Pradyumna and Aniruddha could not save the child, and curses Arjuna's boasting. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 28-40)

title: Krishna Leads Arjuna to Vaikuntha
one_line_summary: Krishna, to save the despairing Arjuna, mounts his divine chariot and carries him beyond the darkness to Vaikuntha, where they behold the Supreme Lord upon the serpent Ananta.
source_excerpt: Restraining Arjuna from entering the fire, Krishna mounts his divine chariot and drives westward across the seven continents and seas, beyond the mountain Lokaloka into the great darkness, where he sends his blazing discus to cleave the gloom. Passing through, they behold the Supreme Lord, radiant like a mountain of light, reclining upon the thousand-headed serpent Ananta, and both Krishna and Arjuna bow to him. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 41-56)

title: The Lost Sons Returned
one_line_summary: The Supreme Lord tells Krishna and Arjuna that he himself had taken the brahmana's sons to bring them together, and returns the children, whom they restore to the brahmana.
source_excerpt: The Supreme Lord tells Krishna and Arjuna that he, wishing to see them, had himself brought the brahmana's sons to his abode, and that having slain the earth's burden they should now return. Taking the children, Krishna and Arjuna return by the way they came and restore the sons to the brahmana, and Arjuna, astounded at the vision of Vishnu's abode, regards all human power as Krishna's grace. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 57-61)

title: Krishna's Water-Sports with His Queens
one_line_summary: Krishna sports in the lakes with his sixteen thousand wives, splashing and being splashed, while the women's songs of longing express their single-hearted devotion.
source_excerpt: Krishna, delighting in Dwaraka, sports with his sixteen thousand wives, bathing and playing in the lakes, splashing them as they splash him, like the lord of the yakshas among his yakshinis. The queens, wholly devoted to Krishna, pour out songs of longing to the birds, the moon, the wind and the clouds, and by such constant love attain the supreme state. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1-24)
notes: Sensual imagery; age_sensitivity set to mild.

title: Krishna's Sons and the Yadu Lineage
one_line_summary: The text enumerates Krishna's sixteen thousand wives and his many sons — Pradyumna, Aniruddha and others — and traces the line through Vajra, the sole Yadu survivor of the coming internecine war.
source_excerpt: Krishna has sixteen thousand and more than a hundred queens, and on each he begets ten sons; among the foremost are Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Samba and others. Pradyumna's grandson through Aniruddha is Vajra, who alone would survive the destruction by the mace, and the Yadava line is declared too vast to count. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 28-45)
